questions.q: Under local authentication, which system checks the username and password?
options: An external Identity Provider
ServiceNow itself, validating against sys_user
The user's own browser
No check happens; local authentication skips password validation
questions.explain: Local authentication means ServiceNow stores and validates credentials directly against the sys_user table, with no external party involved.

questions.q: What does ServiceNow do differently under SSO compared to local authentication?
options: It deletes the sys_user table entirely
It stops enforcing any roles or ACLs
It delegates credential checking to an external Identity Provider and trusts that IdP's confirmation instead of checking the password itself
It requires the user to type their password twice
questions.explain: Under SSO, ServiceNow becomes a consumer of a confirmed identity from the IdP rather than the system that verifies the password directly.

questions.q: Of the three enterprise reasons for moving to SSO, which one is identified as the argument that usually matters most?
options: Faster page load times inside ServiceNow
Offboarding — disabling one IdP account cuts off access to every connected system at once
It removes the need for any user records in ServiceNow
It allows skipping role design entirely
questions.explain: With local authentication, offboarding requires separately disabling a user in every connected application; SSO consolidates that into one action at the IdP.

questions.q: A user logs in through SSO. What still determines what they're allowed to do inside ServiceNow once they're authenticated?
options: Nothing — SSO users bypass all ACLs automatically
Their roles, group memberships, and the same ACL evaluation covered in Chapters 1 and 2
Whatever permissions the IdP happens to list, ignoring ServiceNow's own role model
SSO users are always granted security_admin by default
questions.explain: Authentication and authorization are separate layers — SSO changes how identity is confirmed, but roles, ACLs, and group membership still govern access exactly as before.

questions.q: Why is centralized password policy listed as a real enterprise reason to adopt SSO?
options: Because ServiceNow cannot otherwise enforce any password rules
Because enforcing one password policy at the IdP automatically applies to every connected application, instead of managing separate policies per system
Because it eliminates the need for passwords altogether
Because it only applies to ServiceNow and no other application
questions.explain: An organization with many applications benefits from enforcing complexity, lockout, and expiration rules once at the IdP rather than separately in each connected system.
